aChorusOfSuffering.title: Scenario IV-C: A Chorus of Suffering

intro.title: Scenario IV-C: A Chorus of Suffering
intro.part1: On a day like this, Naples looks like something out of a dream. An impossibly blue sky hangs over the shimmering bay, and your fellow passengers chatter pleasantly amongst themselves as they disembark from your train at Napoli Campi Flegrei station. The gentle sea breeze and beautiful atmosphere are almost enough to make you forget why you came here—to find one of the three witches that want your head on a platter. Almost, but not quite.
intro.part2:
From the station, it’s a quick cab ride up to Vomero Hill. There were no buildings in your vision, and the walnut tree was smaller, younger. But as you squint toward the horizon, you're sure this is the place. You lean against the old walnut tree, staring out over the city and across the bay, and wonder— not for the first time—if you've lost your mind chasing this half-baked vision across the sea.

You weren't sure what you expected to happen when you got here, but when your vision suddenly dims and the world turns to shades of gray, you're certain that this wasn’t it. A storm of biblical proportions has swallowed Naples. The city below you drowns under the downpour, as enormous waves from the bay swallow entire streets. The walnut tree behind you cracks under the pounding rain and topples, missing you by inches. You can only watch in horror as the city sinks beneath the flood—except for one building, untouched by the storm. A theater.

As quickly as it came, the vision is gone. The sun is back, warm on your skin. Everything is as it was—including the theater from your vision, down in the San Ferdinando district. You narrow your eyes. Your last vision had you cross the globe to see it through—at least this one isn’t asking you to travel quite so far.
intro.part3: Your friends in the underworld have provided you with plenty of information on Amalia Verdi to review over the course of your long train ride. A distant relation of the late and great Giuseppe Verdi, Amalia is twenty-three years old and a rising star in the world of opera. Her voice has taken much of Europe by storm, but you know her success isn’t simply due to her natural talent. Amalia’s management has been bankrolled almost entirely by her mentor, Madame Ana Giuliano. Of course, you know that Giuliano hasn't been funnelling all of the cash she’s gleaned from the Boston Mob into this girl’s career out of the goodness of her heart. No, whatever Madame Giuliano’s endgame is, it’s got nothing to do with music. You just don’t know what that is, yet, Amalia is set to perform at the Teatro di San Carlo for the next month, taking on the role of a lifetime—Brunnhilde, in Wagner's Die Walküre. Getting a face-to-face with her won't be easy, but you need to figure out the truth behind her connection to Giuliano if you have any hope of figuring out how to stop the Three Mothers.
intro.part4:
Your borrowed copy of Our Ladies of Sorrow sits comfortably in your luggage as you think back to the evening you and Dr. Armitage had spent poring over its contents. Brother Ross's writings on Mater Lachrymarum—the Mother of Tears, the most powerful of the Sorrows—were fevered, as though the very act of putting quill to parchment strained his sanity. In a trembling hand, Ross had written of a place where “the Weeping Mother reigns supreme—from whose tears the witches are born, who spit in the face of Aradia, the rightful heir; who defiles the sacred walnut tree.” The place he named was Benevento, a city long thought of as the epicenter of witchcraft in medieval Europe. Yet when you presented the revelation to Dr. Armitage, you found him skeptical you'd find Mater Lachrymarum there today.

‘You see, between the 15th and 17th centuries the Church launched brutal witch hunts in Benevento, determined to wipe out the covens that had taken root there. Many were caught, tortured, and executed, but many more survived. The witches of Benevento didn’t die off—they simply moved.” Armitage tapped a map of Italy spread out on the table before you for emphasis, before moving his finger south, to point at the city of Naples. “Benevento may have been where witchcraft began, but Naples is where it still thrives. If Mater Lachrymarum is to be found anywhere in Italy, it’s there.”
intro.part5:
The last words you shared with Anna Kaslow still echo in your mind. Her voice had taken on a somber tone when the time came for her to divulge what she knew about Mater Lachrymarum, the most powerful of the Three Mothers. “It's been a long time since I dared to speak her name,” Anna had said, taking a sip of long-cold tea. “You think you understand you're dealing with? You don’t. I wasn’t just a follower, you know. I wasn't some starry-eyed devotee offering up empty prayers. No... I was her disciple. I belonged to her. A daughter of sorrow. When you've lived with nothing but pain and grief, the idea of surrendering to it, of letting it consume you... it can be seductive. She comes for the broken, the bereaved. And when she does...”

“lived in her grasp for years. Decades, maybe. Time doesn’t work the same when you're under her influence. You lose yourself...” Anna’s expression had become distant, as though she was reliving those terrible years all over again. “... You know, used to think I'd won my freedom, fair and square. That I'd somehow survived, when so many others hadn't. But maybe she only let me leave so I could tell you this story. So Id warn you... and so she can enjoy your failure that much more.” Anna stood slowly, her voice barely more than a whisper. “If you're searching for her, you'll find her in Italy—in Naples. But you won't be facing a witch. You'll be facing the embodiment of despair itself. And you won't survive.”

Anna offered you one last smile before pushing open the tiny door of her shop. “Now, get out. And don't ever come back.”
intro.part6:
The facade of the Teatro di San Carlo glitters like starlight in the fading evening light. You've managed to secure the last remaining tickets for this evening's performance of Wagner's Die Walküre. The halls inside are lined with posters—rich, colorful illustrations of the evening's performers. Most of them showcase the beautiful, haunting image of this evening’s Brunnhilde: the opera star Amalia Verdi, her face beautiful and serene. As you take your seats and the curtain rises, the hum of excitement that fills the theatre begins to reach a boiling point. You're not sure what to expect from the performance, but enjoying the show isn’t your aim—your plan is to search the theatre from top to bottom in search of Mater Lachrymarum once the show is over.

While the performance progresses to its second act, your chest begins to tighten, and a sharp pain lances through your temples. At first, you think it’s the music—but no, this is something else. The pain is unbearable. From the corner of your vision, you glimpse a figure offstage, watching Amalia’s performance with hungry eyes. You strain to focus, but the figure flickers like an image on the edge of a dream. It's impossible, but... could that be Ana Giuliano? The pain sharpens. Your head spins, your vision goes dark, and then—nothing.

When you awaken, the theater around you is no longer the gilded palace it once was—it’s crumbling. Moss creeps up the cracked walls, and the velvet seats are slick with rot. Outside, you can see the reason for the decay. Naples lies submerged beneath a sea of black water. Only the tops of buildings remain visible above the flood. The streets, the people, all gone—consumed by the waves. The ceiling of the theater sags under the weight of heavy rainfall, and water laps at your ankles—and it is rising. Rapidly.

And somewhere, echoing through the hollowed-out theater, you hear a voice. Amalia’s voice, sweet and lilting. She’s singing. “Confess your sins,” she echoes, beckoning. “Lay down your burdens.”

The water is up to your knees now. You have to move.
intro.part7:
Gigi stands dumbfounded, trembling, as the water rises around her. Her knuckles are white against the rotten seat in front of her. “Did you see him?” she gasps, frantic. “Did you see Jackie? He was on the stage, with her— with Ana... !” Her voice breaks at the mention of her husband, and the woman who’s led all of you into this mess. “We have to find him,” she pleads, her voice barely audible over Amalia’s song. “Please. I can't lose him now.”

There’s no time for explanations, no time to question whether the things you and Gigi see are real or just another part of this nightmare. It's time to go.

rules.title: The Deluge, The Depths & The Deck of Burdens
rules.body:
Throughout this scenario, the number of resources under “The Deluge” on the scenario reference card indicates the current Deluge level. As the investigators survive the rising tides by completing Act 1, resources are added to the current Deluge level. The current Deluge level has no game effect on its own; however, some encounter card effects may change or become stronger depending on the current depth level.

Some cards in this scenario reference an area called “the Depths.” The Depths is an out-of-play area next to the act and agenda deck that enemies can enter and leave via card effects. Generally speaking, enemies in play will move to the Depths whenever the investigators reach the next Deluge level. Although the Depths are out of play, whenever an enemy moves to the Depths, it keeps all tokens and attachments unless otherwise specified. Enemies in the Depths are considered to be out of play, and cannot be affected by player cards or investigator actions. However, enemies that are in the Depths can re-enter play by a variety of scenario card abilities.

The Deck of Burdens is a set of 8 weaknesses with the Burden trait required to play A Chorus of Suffering. These cards cannot be permanently added to an investigator’s deck. Instead, when the investigators are instructed to construct the Teatro di San Carlo (either during setup or when advancing Act 1A), all Burden cards in play return to the Deck of Burdens, are shuffled together, and are then distributed face down amongst the cards that make up each new level of the Teatro di San Carlo.
